EU Greenwashing Rules Take Effect With Fines Exceeding 4% of Turnover
- Financial exposure: EU Member States can impose greenwashing penalties exceeding 4% of annual turnover for serious breaches, depending on national enforcement rules.
- Stricter environmental claims: New restrictions prohibit unsubstantiated claims such as “eco” and “sustainable”, alongside carbon neutrality claims based on offsetting.
- Existing inventory: EU regulators have proposed a proportionate enforcement approach for products manufactured, ordered or distributed before the 27 September deadline.
EU Tightens Enforcement of Environmental Marketing Claims
Brussels has introduced stricter consumer protection rules targeting corporate greenwashing, exposing businesses to substantial financial penalties for misleading environmental claims.
The EU’s Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive (ECGT) became applicable on 27 September 2026. It prohibits several common environmental marketing practices, including unsupported sustainability labels and misleading carbon neutrality claims.
National authorities will oversee enforcement, with the most serious violations potentially attracting fines exceeding 4% of annual turnover.
EU regulators have also published a “common understanding” outlining a proportionate approach to existing inventory. The guidance addresses products manufactured, ordered, distributed or placed on retail shelves before the September deadline.
For multinational businesses, the changes create immediate compliance challenges across product packaging, advertising, sustainability communications and supply chains.
Generic Green Claims Face New Restrictions
The directive targets environmental claims that cannot be supported by recognised evidence.
Terms such as “eco” and “sustainable” face restrictions when companies cannot demonstrate the environmental performance implied by their marketing.
The legislation also prohibits claims suggesting products have neutral, reduced or positive greenhouse gas impacts based on carbon offsetting.
Corporate commitments concerning future environmental performance face additional scrutiny.
Companies advertising future “net zero” performance must support those claims with publicly available implementation plans. Independent experts must verify the commitments, with their findings made publicly accessible.
Businesses also cannot present compliance with minimum legal environmental requirements as a distinctive sustainability advantage.
These provisions increase pressure on marketing, legal and sustainability departments to align consumer-facing communications with verifiable environmental performance.
Existing Stock Receives Proportionate Regulatory Treatment
One of the most commercially significant developments concerns products already circulating through European supply chains.
EU regulators have proposed a proportionate approach to goods manufactured, ordered, distributed or stocked before 27 September.
The guidance recognises the practical difficulties of immediately replacing packaging and labels across extensive retail inventories.
However, this approach should not be interpreted as a blanket exemption from the new requirements.
Companies must distinguish between existing inventory and newly produced materials while monitoring how individual Member States apply enforcement measures.
For manufacturers and retailers, the distinction could influence inventory management, packaging expenditure and contractual arrangements with suppliers.
Packaging Rules Add Another Compliance Layer
The EU’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) introduced further restrictions from 12 August 2026.
Environmental claims concerning recyclability and recycled content must exceed minimum regulatory requirements.
Businesses must also clarify whether claims apply to individual packaging units or their broader packaging portfolios.
RELATED ARTICLE: EU Commission Proposes Rules to Protect Consumers from Greenwashing
These obligations will evolve as additional PPWR provisions become applicable.
Companies operating across multiple European markets face increasing pressure to standardise environmental claims while accommodating national enforcement practices.
UK Advertising Rulings Reinforce Scrutiny
Regulatory action is also intensifying outside the EU.
The UK’s Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) recently ruled against travel agencies Thomas Cook, loveholidays and DialAFlight over inadequately explained environmental advertising claims.
Advertisements describing hotels as “eco” or “eco-conscious” failed to provide sufficient information about the environmental characteristics supporting those descriptions.
The ASA also upheld complaints against Eurowings and Qatar Airways concerning speculative carbon offsetting claims.
Regulators found that the advertisements could mislead consumers about the environmental impact of individual flights.
Meanwhile, the UK Law Commission is examining a potential consumer class actions regime. Its consultation closes on 30 October.
Such a framework could increase corporate litigation exposure for misleading sustainability claims.
Financial and Governance Implications for Global Businesses
The EU’s enforcement framework raises the financial consequences of unsupported environmental marketing.
For executives, compliance now extends beyond sustainability reporting into product development, procurement, advertising approvals and corporate governance.
Investors must also consider whether companies maintain adequate controls over environmental claims across international markets.
The combination of turnover-based penalties, stricter substantiation requirements and potential litigation creates material legal and reputational exposure.
For businesses selling into Europe, credible sustainability communication increasingly depends on documented performance rather than broad environmental positioning.
The EU’s approach could also influence regulatory expectations internationally, particularly as authorities examine the credibility of corporate climate commitments and consumer-facing environmental claims.

articles.title: SJ Fall Summit: What Does Human Rights Due Diligence Look Like in 2026? - WWD
articles.summary: SJ Fall Summit: What Does Human Rights Due Diligence Look Like in 2026?  WWD
articles.full_text:
For two decades, supply chain transparency has largely been a voluntary exercise. Audit reports, supplier codes of conduct and corporate sustainability pledges have made up the bulk of brands’ efforts to push a more ecological and socially aware agenda, but times have changed.
With European Union directives such as the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, or CSDDD, and the Forced Labor Regulation, or FLR, going into effect in 2027, brands are being forced to shift to a new paradigm of active accountability, according to Jasmin Malik Chua, Sourcing Journal’s climate and labor editor, who moderated a discussion about what human rights due diligence looks like in 2026 at the Sourcing Journal Fall Summit on Sept. 29.
New legal and regulatory standards mean brands are “really entering a new era” when it comes to compliance, according to Shawn MacDonald, CEO of Verité, an advisory, research and advocacy group. “For so long, if company wasn’t a really well-known household name that might get the attention of an editor at The New York Times to get on the front page, or by an attack by a particular advocacy group, they could essentially assume that they wouldn’t get into much trouble.”
Now, though, there are “a proliferation of import prohibitions…for goods made with forced labor,” and that means “we have a threat calculus that’s deeper, wider, more legal and more financial.” Companies are being held to account for their procurement practices like never before.
“If you get caught by U.S. Customs and Border Protection now, it’s essentially millions and millions of dollars in remedy,” he added, referencing violations of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, which took effect in 2022.
The EU will begin enforcing its own forced labor import ban next year, and with 60 economies targeted by the Trump administration’s Section 301 investigation and subsequent tariff penalty based on allegations of lax import regulation, MacDonald believes they will adopt similar provisions. That spells greater risk for companies selling into global markets.
The executive believes that with increased adoption of AI by enforcement agencies, companies could become “susceptible to being spotlighted” and scrutinized. Advocacy groups, unions and other due diligence bodies are only advancing in their capabilities and capacity to root out wrongdoing. Brands that invest in mapping their supply chains and ensuring compliance will be better positioned to weather these shifts.
Asked whether, in this new regulatory era, brands could recognize the benefits of treating worker organizations as strategic compliance partners, Kelly M. Fay Rodríguez, executive director of the Competence Center for Human Rights Due Diligence and former U.S. Special Representative for International Labor Affairs at the State Department, said, “As a proper optimist, I think companies are going to get it.”
“If you want to protect your supply chain, you’re going to engage unions. Period,” she added. State and local, national and global union federations represent workers across global value chains, and even in locales that prohibit unions or engage in union-busting, there are labor actors that brands can partner with to ensure freedom of association, she said.
IndustriAll Global Union Federation and UNI Global Union Federation, which both represent workers in the fashion industry, are invaluable resources for brands, she added. “They know the risks that exist in countries around the world, from manufacturing fabrics to stitching to dyeing, to shipping, selling goods at the storefronts, and they can be crucial stakeholders for you for companies that want to avoid the chaos, that want to avoid the unpredictability of enforcement, and/or simply want more sustainable supply chains,” Rodríguez said. “They want more resilient and profitable supply chains.”
Brands would do well to engage as many resources as they can wrangle to aid in their efforts to achieve and maintain compliance, according to Marissa Brock, senior director of policy at Sourcemap Inc. But if they’re feeling behind, it’s not too late.
“One would hope that brands have been conducting these due diligence processes now for years. But let’s say that they have not. Some have not. There really is quite a bit of time now to get these processes in place,” she said. Full application and compliance for the CSDDD, for example, takes effect in 2029, and reporting requirements begin in 2030. Full enforcement of the FLR begins earlier, in December 2027, but there’s still more than a year of runway for firms that are proactive.
“Advice that I frequently give to a lot of the companies that we work with is that there are a lot of pieces of legislation now that have overlapping requirements, not just on the human rights side, but on the environmental risk side as well. The goal should be to find the path of least resistance in terms of data collection to make sure that you are collecting that data in as efficient a way as possible,” Brock said.
Streamlining the process of coalescing supply chain insights will help brands not just with the regulations coming down the pike, but those that will inevitably follow.
“The more cumbersome you make that data collection process, the less likely your company is to really adopt those processes, and then the less compliant you will be,” Brock said. “So, that really is the advice that I would I would share: Start as soon as humanly possible.”

articles.title: Green Claims, Real Consequences: What the EU’s New Greenwashing Rules Mean for Businesses - The National Law Review
articles.summary: Green Claims, Real Consequences: What the EU’s New Greenwashing Rules Mean for Businesses  The National Law Review
articles.full_text:
Since 27 September 2026, businesses selling to consumers in the European Union (“EU”) have been subject to new rules on environmental claims. The rules come from the EU’s Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive (EU) 2024/825 (the “EmpCo Directive”), which amends the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (2005/29/EC) (“UCPD”) and the Consumer Rights Directive (2011/83/EU) (“CRD”). These new rules intend to strengthen EU consumer protection against greenwashing and are applicable to all businesses – regardless of size, number of employees, or annual turnover, and including those based outside the EU – selling to EU consumers.
The rules are already in effect, with no transition period. This change matters beyond consumer brands: the rules should now be factored into due diligence on M&A deals involving a business that sells to EU consumers (see Question 2), and they are relevant to asset managers whose fund marketing, or whose portfolio companies’ claims, reach EU consumers (see Question 3).
The EmpCo Directive at a glance
- Who is in scope? Any business that markets or sells to consumers in the EU, in any sector and wherever it is based. This includes financial services firms and anyone acting on a business’s behalf, such as distributors or agencies. Dealings purely between businesses are not in scope.
- Which products? Almost anything offered to consumers, including goods, services (including financial products), digital content and property. The rules apply to everything a consumer sees before, during and after a sale – packaging, labels, advertising, websites, social media and brand or product names – including stock already on shelves.
- When can you call something “green”? Only when the claim can be backed up. In particular:
  - general claims such as “eco-friendly”, “green” or “climate-friendly” are banned outright unless the business can show recognised excellent environmental performance, or the claim is clearly explained on the same label or advert;
  - sustainability labels must be based on an independently verified certification scheme or set up by a public authority;
  - a claim about a whole product or business must be true of the whole, not just one part of it;
  - products cannot be described as “carbon neutral”, or as having a reduced or positive climate impact, on the basis of carbon offsetting; and
  - future targets such as net zero must be backed by a detailed, public plan with measurable deadlines, checked regularly by an independent expert.
Below, we answer three key questions clients may need to navigate.
Question 1: We are a US company selling products into the EU. Do we need controls in place?
Yes. What matters is where your customers are, not where your business is based. If a business markets or sells to consumers in the EU, the rules will apply, whether it sells through an EU subsidiary, a distributor, an online marketplace, or its own website.
The main risk for US businesses is using marketing created for the US market in the EU without adapting it. Some claims that may be acceptable in the US may not be permitted in the EU.
We recommend the following practical steps:
- Know what you are saying: Build a list of every environmental or social claim used with EU consumers across packaging, websites, social media and advertising. Include brand and product names, and images or colours that suggest green credentials.
- Check your labels: Confirm that every sustainability label or logo is backed by a proper certification scheme or a public authority. Do not assume a well-known label is automatically compliant.
- Remove high-risk claims: Drop vague green wording such as “eco-friendly” or “green” where you cannot demonstrate “recognised excellent environmental performance”, and any product claims based on carbon offsetting.
- Take care with net zero and other targets: If future targets are mentioned in consumer marketing, they need to be backed by a clear, public plan with measurable milestones that is regularly checked by an independent expert.
- Put sign-off in place: Require legal and sustainability review before any new EU-facing claim goes live, and keep evidence on file for each claim.
- Watch what you reuse: Statements taken from sustainability reports and reused in consumer marketing can be caught by the rules.
Businesses selling to EU consumers should be reviewing their policies and procedures and, where appropriate, implement additional controls over their consumer-facing claims.
Question 2: How will the EmpCo Directive affect mergers & acquisitions?
For any deal involving a business that sells to EU consumers, these rules should now be part of standard due diligence. There are three main issues: getting the scope right, valuing the risk, and protecting the buyer in the deal documents.
Getting the scope right
The EmpCo Directive has not changed the general scope of the UCPD. The UCPD applies to unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices before, during and after a commercial transaction in relation to a ‘product’. This is a broad concept covering goods, services, immovable property, rights and obligations. Purely business-to-business practices remain outside scope.
Below are a few common assumptions which businesses will need to watch out for:
- “The target isn’t based in the EU.” That does not matter if it sells to EU consumers.
- “The target only sells to businesses.” Business-only communications are outside the rules. However, if the target’s customers pass its environmental claims on to consumers, the target may still face contractual claims and commercial pressure.
- “The stock was made before the rules came in.” The new requirements apply to pre-existing materials, including stock and packaging already shipped to retailers and remaining unsold. Any leniency from regulators is discretionary and likely to be narrow.
- “The relevant country hasn’t brought in its law yet.” Member States had to bring the rules into national law by 27 March 2026, but progress has been uneven. Where a country is late, regulators can still act against misleading green claims under existing national consumer laws, and national courts are expected to interpret those laws in line with the EmpCo Directive. However, the EmpCo Directive cannot itself impose obligations on private businesses where it has not yet been transposed into national law. The position should therefore be checked country by country for each market where the target sells.
- “The brand name is a registered trademark”. Brand and product names can themselves be environmental claims, and trademark protection is no defence.
- “The target is a financial business covered by SFDR.” Its wider marketing may still be caught (see Question 3).
It is also worth being clear about what the rules do not cover. They govern how products are described to consumers, not how they are made. Specific, measurable claims that can be substantiated, such as “made with 50% recycled materials”, are still allowed. Due diligence should therefore focus on claims, labels and the evidence behind them.
Valuing the risk
The UCPD and CRD require effective penalties for breaches of the requirements introduced by the EmpCo Directive. Where fines are imposed through coordinated cross-border enforcement, maximum fines must be at least 4% of annual turnover in the Member State concerned. This figure is based on national turnover, not global turnover, but action across several Member States can add up. In practice, the commercial costs often matter more, such as:
- relabelling, repackaging and updating websites;
- writing off stock that cannot be sold as labelled;
- legal action by competitors or consumer associations;
- consumer claims for compensation or price reductions; and/or
- reputational damage.
Warranties and other protections
The impact of the EmpCo Directive will likely flow into warranties. A general warranty that the target has complied with the law may not give a buyer enough comfort. Buyers should consider specific warranties to provide comfort that the rules have been fully complied with.
Sellers will try to limit these warranties to matters within their knowledge and to material issues, and will make disclosures against them. For sellers, reviewing and correcting claims before a sale process begins could limit the protections a buyer will ask for.
Question 3: What does this mean for funds already subject to the EU Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (EU) 2019/2088 (“SFDR”)?
The new EmpCo Directive rules do not change what funds must disclose under SFDR, but complying with SFDR does not automatically mean complying with the EmpCo Directive. Specific financial services rules will take priority where they conflict, however, any sustainability marketing beyond those required disclosures, such as website content, factsheets, social media and promotional material, may be caught by the EmpCo Directive if it reaches consumers.
At fund and manager level
The key question is whether you are dealing with consumers. Funds marketed only to institutional investors are largely outside the rules. However, individuals investing in a personal capacity or acting outside their trade or profession may remain a consumer under the UCPD even if they have opted to be treated as a professional client under MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU, Annex II, Section II).
This consumer question is likely to become more pressing as private markets open up to retail investors. As managers increasingly market and distribute funds to individuals, whether directly or through intermediaries, more of their investor base may fall within the scope of the EmpCo Directive. articles.title: Trump’s SEC is Threatening Big Investors That Pushed ExxonMobil on Climate Risk - Mother Jones
articles.summary: Trump’s SEC is Threatening Big Investors That Pushed ExxonMobil on Climate Risk  Mother Jones
articles.full_text:
This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
The US Securities and Exchange Commission issued an unusual warning this week to the country’s largest asset managers and a climate-focused investor group over their roles in a 2021 campaign that replaced board directors at ExxonMobil.
The commission published a letter saying it had concluded a probe into the entities, and while it found no evidence of violations, it expressed “serious concerns” about their actions.
Investor advocates and some former SEC staff say the letter clearly aims to suppress shareholder advocacy on climate change and pressure large asset managers like BlackRock, State Street, and Vanguard, each of which were named in the letter, to steer clear of the topic entirely.
It is only the latest move by the SEC this year to limit investors’ ability to address climate risks and engage with corporate boards more broadly. The Trump administration and Republican officials across the country have spent years clamping down on efforts to press corporations for climate action.
In 2022, Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives opened an antitrust investigation into some of the same groups, accusing them of acting like a “cartel.” More than a dozen Republican state attorneys general also launched probes. Oil industry campaign contributions have gone overwhelmingly to Republican candidates.
Mika Morse, who was a policy counsel on climate risk to former SEC Chair Gary Gensler, said many investors and asset managers view climate change as a significant risk to their portfolios and feel a fiduciary duty to engage with companies on the topic, but may now hesitate to continue that work.
“Investors are feeling really inhibited because of this fear that they will become the target of investigations,” Morse said. “And this type of harassment is really effective, unfortunately.”
SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock, who began that position in May, was an attorney at Exxon during the investors’ campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. An SEC spokesperson said the investigation began last year and that Woodcock recused himself.
The investigation probed the communications of some of the country’s largest asset managers and pension funds—including BlackRock, State Street, Vanguard, the California Public Employees’ Retirement System, and the New York State Common Retirement Fund—with a group called Climate Action 100+, an investor initiative that pushes for climate action by large corporate emitters.
The report traced what it called a campaign by Climate Action 100+ beginning in 2019 to change Exxon’s board because of the company’s inaction on global warming. The California and New York pension funds were active in the climate group, and BlackRock and State Street joined the initiative in 2020.
By 2021, a small activist investor firm called Engine No. 1 had launched a campaign to replace some of Exxon’s directors. That campaign focused on what the firm said was the company’s poor financial performance—Exxon had been removed from the Dow Jones Industrial Average the previous year as its stock price lagged—rather than inaction on climate change. But the SEC letter said Engine No. 1 had communicated with some Climate Action 100+ members and with Ceres, a sustainable business advocacy group that helps coordinate the climate investor organization.
That year, the campaign succeeded in appointing three new members to Exxon’s board, in large part by convincing large asset managers like BlackRock to vote yes.
It was a huge blow to Exxon and came at a low point for the oil industry. Profits had plummeted during the COVID-19 pandemic. Some analysts were predicting peak oil consumption had passed. Major investors lined up behind the notion that climate risks were systemic, and President Joe Biden had won election the prior year after pledging to shift away from fossil fuels.
In the following years, the oil industry and its allies in public office and think tanks pushed back forcefully, filing lawsuits, launching investigations, and pushing legislation that targeted opponents in the financial sector, academia and elsewhere.
The Trump administration has incorporated this effort as public policy through the Department of Justice, SEC, and other agencies, siding with the oil industry in numerous lawsuits, for example.
The SEC investigation examined whether the asset managers and other members of the climate organization coordinated their votes, which could have triggered onerous reporting requirements under SEC rules meant to give public insight into campaigns by activist investors to influence companies.
Firms like BlackRock are exempt from these reporting requirements even though they hold large stakes in many companies because they are considered passive investors. The SEC letter raised the question of whether the firms should have been required to report more extensively in the case of the Exxon campaign.
Experts in securities law say the difference is significant and that a finding of violation could have had serious implications. Ultimately, the commission did not find evidence to support any of these claims but still issued a public report.
Jim Moloney, director of the SEC’s Division of Corporation Finance, said the “report reminds asset managers and investors of their responsibilities with respect to shareholder engagement, especially in the context of organized efforts that follow a playbook similar to that of Climate Action 100+.”
Shareholder advocates have criticized the SEC report, arguing that it sought to intimidate investors. “What we’ve seen in the ongoing investigations and attacks on climate groups is simply an opinion that shareholders should not be considering climate,” said Danielle Fugere, president and chief counsel of As You Sow, a nonprofit shareholder advocacy group that is part of the Climate Action 100+. “This is just part of this pressure campaign to ensure that the financial system doesn’t take climate into account.”
Andrew Behar, As You Sow’s chief executive, said the campaign to remake Exxon’s board was an attempt to reverse the company’s declining financial performance, and it worked. He pointed to a sustained increase in Exxon’s value that coincided with the addition of new board members.
Overall, Behar said, the campaign showed how capitalism is meant to work.
Michael Boudett, general counsel at Ceres, said in a statement, “Climate Action 100+ has always operated within US securities law. It supports investors as they assess and address the financial risks that climate poses to the companies they invest in. It is up to every participating Climate Action 100+ investor to make their own decisions, including how they vote their shares.”
He added, “Understanding material risks, including financial risks from climate change, is central to that duty.”
Many shareholder advocates have criticized the SEC more broadly under the Trump administration. It is generally supposed to have five commissioners with at least two from each party, but there are currently only two total, and President Donald Trump has not appointed any Democratic commissioners. Last week, the commission issued a rule saying it can reach a quorum with only one commissioner.
BlackRock and State Street declined to comment, with a BlackRock spokesperson pointing to the SEC report’s declaration that the investigation “did not develop evidence that BlackRock or State Street agreed to vote proxies in certain manners or shared their proxy voting intentions with investors or others associated with” the Climate Action 100+.
Exxon did not respond to a request for comment.
As conservatives have targeted BlackRock, its positions have shifted. The asset manager left the Climate Action 100+ in 2024. Behar said that a few years ago, BlackRock voted in favor of nearly half the proposals his organization supported, which cover numerous social and environmental topics. Last year BlackRock backed hardly any.
Morse said the SEC has identified all the ways investors try to press companies to manage climate risk and is working to shut down each path, from limiting their ability to file shareholder resolutions to making it harder for investors to meet with companies.
“The total picture is pretty stunning,” Morse said.
After the commission proposed rescinding a rule on climate-related disclosures, Morse said she heard from many investors and people at corporations that they disagreed with the proposal but declined to submit comments because they feared retribution.
While she understood their position, she said, “This is such a low point for our democracy, that companies and investors would disagree with a policy but be afraid to comment.”

articles.summary: Growthpoint Properties Australia Releases FY26 Sustainability Report, Confirms Net Zero Target Achieved 1 July 2025  Kalkine
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- Net Zero target achieved on 1 July 2025 for all scope 1 and scope 2 emissions from 100% owned directly managed operationally controlled office assets and some scope 3 emissions from corporate activities
- Average NABERS Energy rating across the office portfolio increased to 5.3 stars, from 5.2 stars at 30 June 2022
- 1,610 kW of solar capacity installed since FY22, bringing total capacity across Growthpoint's direct portfolio to 5,817 kW
- First portfolio-wide climate scenario analysis completed to support preparation for mandatory climate-related reporting
- New FY27–FY30 Sustainability Strategy launched, focused on the themes of Resilient, Engaged and Responsible
Net Zero Achievement and Carbon Credit Methodology
According to the filing, Growthpoint achieved its Group Net Zero target on 1 July 2025, covering all scope 1 and scope 2 emissions from its 100% owned directly managed operationally controlled office assets and some scope 3 emissions from corporate activities. The company proactively purchased and retired carbon credits to offset the majority of its forecast FY26 greenhouse gas emissions that could not be avoided or reduced. The remaining credits required to fully offset FY26 emissions were purchased and retired upon finalisation of the Group's greenhouse gas inventory, the filing states.
Portfolio Energy and Solar Capacity Disclosures
The FY26 Sustainability Report discloses that the average NABERS Energy rating across Growthpoint's office portfolio reached 5.3 stars, compared with 5.2 stars recorded at 30 June 2022. The company also disclosed that 1,610 kW of solar capacity has been installed since FY22, bringing the total solar capacity across its direct portfolio to 5,817 kW. The report additionally notes the completion of Growthpoint's first portfolio-wide climate scenario analysis, undertaken to support climate resilience and preparation for mandatory climate-related reporting.
Reporting Standards and New Sustainability Strategy
The FY26 Sustainability Report, described in the filing as Growthpoint's 11th annual report of this kind, has been prepared with reference to the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards and the Australian Sustainability Reporting Standard AASB S2 Climate-related Disclosures. The filing notes Growthpoint is not required to prepare a sustainability report under Chapter 2M of the Corporations Act 2001 until the year ended 30 June 2027. Selected environmental data has been subject to limited assurance by Ernst & Young. The company also disclosed the launch of its FY27–FY30 Sustainability Strategy, focused on the themes of Resilient, Engaged and Responsible.

articles.full_text:
Sustainability Reporting Expands Directors’ ESG Duties, ECGI Study Finds
- Board accountability: Mandatory sustainability reporting is expanding directors’ oversight responsibilities, even without new fiduciary duties.
- Regulatory divergence: The UK has three legal channels for ESG oversight, Singapore has two, and Delaware effectively has one.
- Corporate governance: Researchers recommend clearer oversight duties, legal protections for uncertain disclosures, proportionate assurance, and cross-border regulatory recognition.
Mandatory sustainability reporting is changing what corporate directors must oversee, even where company law has not introduced new ESG obligations.
A September 2026 working paper from the European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) examines how disclosure requirements increasingly influence directors’ legal responsibilities.
Authored by Luh Luh Lan, Associate Professor at the National University of Singapore, the study identifies a mechanism termed the “disclosure-duty feedback loop.”
The central finding challenges a longstanding distinction between corporate transparency and governance. As companies disclose sustainability risks, targets, and oversight arrangements, those disclosures increasingly shape expectations of board conduct.
The result is greater accountability for governance processes, although directors remain legally distinct from guarantors of environmental outcomes.
How Sustainability Reporting Changes Board Responsibilities
The study argues that mandatory reporting creates obligations extending beyond publishing sustainability information.
Companies must establish reliable data collection, verification, and internal control systems. Directors must oversee these processes and understand the environmental and social risks behind reported figures.
Over time, published disclosures establish benchmarks against which future board decisions can be assessed.
A company reporting detailed climate oversight arrangements may subsequently face scrutiny if those arrangements deteriorate or remain unimplemented.
The paper describes this progression as a feedback loop. Reporting obligations shape governance practices, while previous disclosures influence expectations of future oversight.
Importantly, the mechanism operates through existing directors’ duties rather than creating an independent legal obligation to achieve particular ESG outcomes.
UK, Singapore and US Rules Create Different Legal Exposure
The research examines three regulatory approaches: International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) frameworks, European sustainability reporting requirements, and US disclosure rules.
ISSB standards provide a common baseline across jurisdictions including Singapore and the UK.
In Singapore, listed companies must report Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions from financial year 2025. Straits Times Index constituents face Scope 3 requirements from 2026.
The UK published its sustainability reporting standards in February 2026. Regulators have consulted on mandatory implementation beginning in 2027.
Meanwhile, the European Union has narrowed its Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive through Omnibus I.
The revised framework generally targets companies exceeding 1,000 employees and €450 million in turnover.
Despite reduced coverage, the EU retains double materiality. Companies within scope must assess both financial sustainability risks and their impacts on people and the environment.
The US presents a contrasting approach.
Federal climate disclosure requirements face proposed rescission, while California continues advancing emissions reporting obligations for qualifying businesses operating within the state.
These differences create overlapping compliance responsibilities for multinational companies.

Directors Face Growing Accountability for Climate Data
The study identifies significant differences in how existing legal duties translate into ESG accountability.
UK directors face three potential channels of responsibility, including fiduciary obligations, environmental considerations under Section 172, and duties of care.
Singapore provides two channels through fiduciary obligations and duties of care.
Delaware primarily relies on oversight obligations under the duty of loyalty, where establishing liability generally requires demonstrating bad faith.
These distinctions matter when companies face allegations involving inaccurate emissions reporting, inadequate controls, or misleading transition plans.
Scope 3 emissions present particular challenges because companies frequently depend on estimates and information supplied by third parties.
The research argues that reasonable oversight processes should protect directors when estimates subsequently prove inaccurate.
Four Reforms Could Strengthen Corporate ESG Governance
The paper proposes four regulatory reforms to address growing uncertainty.
These include clearer definitions of directors’ oversight responsibilities and safe harbours for good-faith forward-looking statements and Scope 3 estimates.
It also recommends proportionate assurance requirements and mutual recognition between equivalent reporting regimes.
For executives and investors, the findings carry practical implications.
Boards increasingly need documented oversight processes, credible sustainability data, and clear accountability across management functions.
Audit committees may also assume greater responsibility as sustainability disclosures become subject to independent assurance.
The wider challenge concerns regulatory fragmentation.
Companies operating across multiple jurisdictions face different disclosure standards, enforcement mechanisms, and interpretations of directors’ duties.
The ECGI analysis concludes that sustainability reporting is strengthening governance expectations without fundamentally rewriting corporate law.
For multinational boards, the consequences extend beyond compliance. Sustainability disclosures are increasingly becoming part of the legal record against which corporate oversight is judged.

JPMorganChase Updates Climate Targets and Expands Low Carbon Energy Financing
- Climate targets revised: JPMorganChase has updated its portfolio-level carbon intensity targets to align with the International Energy Agency’s 2025 Net Zero Emissions by 2050 scenario.
- Low-carbon financing expanded: The bank has broadened its $2.5 trillion Sustainable Development Target to include grid infrastructure, nuclear energy, and low-carbon activities at diversified power companies.
- Energy strategy strengthened: A new Center for Energy and the Environment will integrate climate expertise, policy engagement, and financing to address barriers to energy investment.
JPMorganChase has revised its climate targets and expanded its definition of low-carbon energy financing as global electricity demand accelerates. The changes reflect a broader strategy that balances decarbonization with energy affordability, security, and reliability.
The U.S. banking giant is also consolidating its energy and sustainability expertise under a new Center for Energy and the Environment (CE&E). The initiative will connect climate targets, financing strategies, and policy engagement across the bank’s operations.
The revisions follow five years of experience implementing portfolio-level carbon intensity targets and a $2.5 trillion Sustainable Development Target established in 2021.
Expanding Low-Carbon Energy Financing
JPMorganChase facilitates nearly $100 billion annually to support new energy supply across multiple sources. Its tax-oriented investment business has also helped finance approximately one-quarter of U.S. renewable energy and storage capacity additions, measured in gigawatts.
The bank is now broadening how it measures capital deployment toward energy and environmental objectives.
Its Sustainable Development Target’s green objective will incorporate additional activities classified as low-carbon under its Energy Supply Financing Ratio (ESFR).
These include electricity grid infrastructure, nuclear energy, and qualifying low-carbon activities undertaken by diversified power companies.
The expansion follows the bank’s 2025 Security and Resiliency Initiative, which prioritizes energy independence and infrastructure resilience.
For investors, the revised framework could direct greater financing attention toward infrastructure essential for electrification and reliable electricity supply.
It also reflects growing recognition that renewable generation requires complementary investments in transmission, storage, and dependable power infrastructure.
Climate Targets Aligned With Updated IEA Pathways
JPMorganChase has updated its portfolio-level carbon intensity targets to reflect the International Energy Agency’s 2025 Net Zero Emissions by 2050 scenario.
The bank describes the scenario as one possible pathway toward achieving net-zero emissions rather than a prediction of future energy demand.
Its targets will continue serving as indicators of portfolio carbon intensity and tools for client engagement.
However, JPMorganChase clarified that it will not restrict financing solely to achieve these targets. Future adjustments remain possible as market conditions and decarbonization pathways evolve.
The approach places greater emphasis on financing activity and energy system development alongside traditional financed-emissions measurements.
The bank argues that financed emissions have limitations, particularly when assessing individual transactions. Inconsistent data, methodological differences, and incomplete disclosures can complicate comparisons.
These limitations raise broader questions for financial institutions seeking to demonstrate credible climate progress while supporting energy-intensive industries.

New Energy Center to Address Investment Barriers
JPMorganChase has combined its Center for Carbon Transition and Corporate Sustainability functions within the new CE&E.
The center will integrate energy policy expertise, environmental strategy, and client engagement.
Heather Zichal, Head of the Center for Energy and the Environment and Global Head of Sustainability, said:
“Meeting energy demand while balancing affordability, security, reliability, and sustainability, what we call the ‘Four Forces,’ is one of the defining economic opportunities of our era.”
The bank identified several obstacles that can delay viable energy projects despite available financing.
These include permitting delays, electricity grid interconnection queues, workforce shortages, supply chain constraints, and uncertain government policies.
CE&E will use JPMorganChase’s relationships with businesses, policymakers, and investors to help address these challenges.
The bank maintains that additional capital alone cannot resolve structural barriers affecting energy infrastructure development.
Implications for Banks and Global Climate Investment
JPMorganChase’s revised strategy comes as financial institutions face competing demands to finance economic growth, strengthen energy security, and support decarbonization.
Its expanded financing framework could increase capital availability for nuclear generation, electricity networks, and other infrastructure supporting lower-carbon energy systems.
However, broader financing classifications also increase the importance of transparent reporting and consistent measurement.
Investors will need to assess whether expanded capital deployment translates into measurable emissions reductions and improved energy resilience.
For corporate leaders, the changes reinforce the importance of aligning decarbonization plans with infrastructure availability, regulatory conditions, and commercial viability.
The wider significance extends beyond U.S. banking. As electricity demand rises globally, financial institutions must increasingly evaluate climate performance alongside energy security and economic competitiveness.
JPMorganChase’s approach illustrates how major lenders are adapting climate strategies to the practical constraints of financing the global energy transition.

articles.title: SFDR opt-out risks fragmented reporting for investors, warns Eurosif - Investment & Pensions Europe
articles.summary: SFDR opt-out risks fragmented reporting for investors, warns Eurosif  Investment & Pensions Europe
articles.full_text:
Plans to let alternative investment funds opt out of the EU’s Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) categorisation framework could leave investors facing inconsistent sustainability disclosures, the European Sustainable Investment Forum (Eurosif) has warned.
Speaking at PRI in Person in Amsterdam, Eurosif executive director Aleksandra Palinska questioned whether the EU’s drive to simplify sustainability reporting had gone too far.
“Simplification should make the framework more effective and easier to implement, not weaken its objectives or create new uncertainty,” she said.
The European Parliament’s negotiating position, adopted in September, would allow alternative investment funds marketed exclusively to professional investors to opt out of the categorisation framework.
For institutional investors, the opt-out could mean greater reliance on separately negotiated disclosures, making it harder to compare managers’ sustainability approaches.
The European Parliament, the Council of the EU and the European Commission are due to begin trilogue negotiations on the revised rules on 22 October, with an agreement targeted by the end of 2026.
Erika Blanckaert, senior public affairs manager and head of sustainability at Invest Europe, said managers would still need to provide investors with sustainability information. She pointed to existing reporting initiatives and disclosure requirements agreed between limited partners (LPs) and general partners (GPs).
However, Sigita Zvirblyte, head of sustainability at private equity firm Livonia Partners, warned that an opt-out could expose managers to competing demands from institutional clients.
“If there is no clear regulation of what should be reported, what we see is that powerful LPs are setting their own standards,” she said, speaking from the audience.
Managers could consequently face multiple reporting templates and requests to calculate similar metrics in different ways, she added.
Blanckaert also questioned whether the proposed fund categories reflected how private-market funds deploy and return capital.
“I think the current SFDR 2.0 compromises just fail to take into account how private markets work,” she said.
It remained unclear when funds would need to meet the proposed 70% alignment threshold, particularly during investment and divestment periods, she added.
PensionsEurope has separately called for greater flexibility for pension funds under SFDR 2.0, arguing that communications with members and beneficiaries should be distinguished from marketing to prospective investors.
Corporate reporting cuts
Cuts to corporate sustainability reporting would leave investors having to fill information gaps through estimates, external data providers and engagement with companies, said Mathilde Dufour, chief sustainability and talent officer at Mirova.
“It also requires us as investors to invest in our internal expertise as well,” she said.
NBIM and investor bodies, including the Dutch Federation of Pension Funds, have previously opposed proposed cuts to corporate disclosures on the financial effects of sustainability issues.
Transition funds
Raoul Köhler, coordinator of sustainable finance at the Netherlands Authority for the Financial Markets (AFM), warned that transition funds could reduce portfolio emissions without delivering corresponding changes in the real economy.
Investors should assess companies’ actions and business strategies alongside their transition targets, he said.
“The risk is that it will deliver products that have paper decarbonisation rather than real-world decarbonisation,” said Köhler.
“What we would really like to see is that product providers are really looking into the transition plans of the underlying companies to ensure that they are really undergoing this transition,” he added.
The French regulator has also called for stronger requirements on transition plans and adverse-impact disclosures under SFDR 2.0.

With the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) nearing implementation, forest products companies must ask whether their compliance processes can provide the evidence needed to demonstrate due diligence.
In 2026, ResourceWise hosted a four-part EUDR Readiness Briefing Series to help industry professionals track regulatory developments, address operational challenges, and assess supply chain traceability.
A key takeaway: readiness requires more than collecting supplier information. Companies must verify material origins, link them to products and shipments, and maintain defensible documentation.
Companies with existing EUDR solutions or internal processes should identify gaps before they affect compliance reporting or EU market access.
A recurring theme was the distinction between established responsible-sourcing practices and the specific evidence EUDR requires.
Forest products companies have long used certification, chain-of-custody systems, legality assessments, and supplier documentation to support sustainable sourcing. These programs offer a valuable foundation but do not, on their own, prove EUDR compliance. Companies must demonstrate that covered products meet the regulation’s deforestation-free and legality requirements, supported by due diligence information.
This means evaluating whether existing programs can provide geolocation evidence, risk assessments, and links between production areas and products sold in the EU. Companies may not need to rebuild their sustainability programs, but must ensure they provide EUDR’s specific, verifiable evidence.
Geolocation was a major operational challenge discussed in the webinars. Collecting coordinates is a starting point, but does not establish the full production area or verify accuracy.
Under EUDR, companies must provide geolocation for relevant production plots. Depending on plot size and type, this may require polygons rather than a single point. For forest-product companies with extensive supplier networks, obtaining accurate polygons can create significant administrative work—especially when suppliers have varying technical capabilities or information must be gathered across many harvest sites.

Having geolocation data is not the same as reliably verifying it. For companies assessing EUDR readiness, existing systems may collect coordinates but lack efficient ways to validate them or use them in downstream reporting.
Unlike supply chains with products traceable to a single production site, forest products pass through multiple stages before reaching their destination. Wood may be harvested, transported to a sawmill, turned into chips or residuals, sent to a pulp mill, and made into paper or packaging. Materials from different origins may be mixed during storage, processing, and manufacturing, making it difficult to link products or shipments to their source areas.
ResourceWise experts emphasized that effective traceability must reflect how wood and fiber move through the supply chain, linking harvest origins, supplier transactions, manufacturing facilities, and finished-product shipments. Sawmill and harvest residuals are especially important: they make up a substantial share of many supply chains, but movement through intermediaries can complicate origin reporting.
EUDR traceability must reflect real production and sourcing practices, not assume a simple path from raw materials to finished products. Companies with existing compliance systems should ask: Can they track mixed fiber, residuals, and multiple sourcing locations without significant manual work?
EUDR readiness depends on supplier participation across the forest products value chain. Even companies with established compliance systems may struggle if suppliers cannot provide consistent, usable information.
ResourceWise's implementation experience shows supplier data availability improving as companies prepare and origin requests become more common. But collecting data is only part of the process: companies also need reliable ways to transmit, validate, organize, and update records.
In the third briefing, Barry Parrish, ResourceWise’s Director of Sustainability, highlighted the value of supplier communication, training, and structured project management. Based on ResourceWise’s experience, communicating requirements, training suppliers to submit data, and collecting geolocation information can take about two months.
Companies should assess not just whether they have the required data, but how efficiently they can obtain missing information and maintain complete records. Those managing extensive supplier networks should ask:
These operational factors determine whether compliance remains manageable as reporting volumes grow.
A final theme was the need to move beyond collecting compliance data and integrate it into daily operations. Accurate harvest-area data, risk assessments, and supplier records must support EUDR-regulated products and shipments by linking origin details to production and shipment records and due diligence documents.
The webinars also discussed the EU's TRACES-based EUDR Information System for submitting due diligence statements. Companies must make these reporting processes operational before commercial shipments require them, including for materials produced before the regulation applies but placed on the EU market afterward. Compliance should therefore inform inventory and shipment planning, not just production.
Overall, EUDR readiness must cover the entire workflow, from supplier data collection to final compliance documentation.
The four-part series reinforced an important distinction between having an EUDR compliance strategy from having a process that reliably supports implementation.
Companies with compliance systems should assess how they perform across real supply chains: Can geolocation be verified? Do origins remain traceable through processing and mixing? Can evidence be linked to shipments and reporting requirements?
They should also evaluate maintenance demands. Workflows reliant on manual data collection, spreadsheets, or repeated supplier requests may be hard to scale.
Rather than simply asking whether a solution exists, forest products companies should ask whether it produces accurate, defensible information efficiently and consistently.

According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Recycled Mixed Metal Scrap market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The World Recycled Mixed Metal Scrap market is an intermediate material stream positioned between metal waste generation and the secondary smelting and refining industry. It consists of heterogeneous ferrous and non-ferrous metal residues recovered from post-consumer and post-industrial sources, including end-of-life vehicles, appliances, electronics, and manufacturing offcuts. Unlike pure single-metal scrap, mixed scrap is commingled and typically contains aluminum, copper, steel, and zinc, often with trace amounts of other metals. This composition makes it a cost-effective feedstock for smelters and refiners, though recovery yields are lower than those of sorted scrap.
The market is global in scope, with major generation in North America, Europe, and Japan, and significant processing demand in China, South Korea, India, and Southeast Asia. Between 2026 and 2035, the market is projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate of 4–6%, driven by circular economy mandates, rising metal demand from electronics and electrical equipment supply chains, and increasing regulatory pressure to divert waste from landfills. articles.title: SFDR 2.0 update - Arthur Cox LLP
articles.summary: SFDR 2.0 update  Arthur Cox LLP
articles.full_text:
Key takeaways
- SFDR 2.0 proposes replacing the existing Article 8 and Article 9 designations with three voluntary categories: Transition, ESG Basics and Sustainable
- Each of the three main categories would be subject to a minimum 70% investment threshold, alongside category-specific criteria and exclusions
- Parliament supports an opt-out from the categorisation regime for AIFs marketed exclusively to per se MiFID professional investors, subject to certain conditions
- Products outside the new categories could continue to provide certain sustainability information, subject to restrictions, and would remain subject to sustainability risk disclosure requirements similar to the existing Article 6 regime
- The proposal remains subject to the EU legislative process and may change before finalisation, with the new regime expected to apply two years after entry into force
SFDR 2.0 proposes the replacement of the existing disclosure regime with three formal product categorisations or labels (Transition, ESG Basics, and Sustainable). The implementation of SFDR has given rise to significant complexity and compliance costs for financial market participants, while also prompting concerns regarding investor protection, legal certainty and the risk of greenwashing. The proposed reforms are intended to simplify the framework, reduce market confusion, enhance the comparability and clarity of sustainability-related disclosures, and ensure greater alignment with other EU sustainable finance initiatives and disclosure regimes.
On 10 September 2026, the Economic and Monetary Affairs (“ECON”) committee of the European Parliament (the “Parliament”) adopted its report on the SFDR 2.0 reforms (PDF, 374 KB), reaching a broad compromise on the proposed text. The European Parliament plenary formally endorsed this report as its negotiating mandate on 5 October 2026, clearing the way for trilogue negotiations between the Parliament, the Council of the EU (the “Council”) and the Commission to begin.
Parliament’s proposed amendments
The ECON committee position supports the Commission’s proposal to introduce three standard product categories, each of which would be required to disclose the principal adverse impacts of its investments on sustainability factors:
- Transition (Article 7 of SFDR 2.0)
- ESG Basics (Article 8 of SFDR 2.0)
- Sustainable (Article 9 of SFDR 2.0)
The ECON committee proposal retains the ability of Transition-category products to invest in companies that generate revenue from fossil fuels, provided that those companies allocate at least 20% of their total capital expenditure to Taxonomy-aligned activities, make significant investments in environmentally sustainable activities and maintain a measurable, time-bound plan to reduce emissions. The proposal adds a further condition: over a rolling three-year period, such companies must also devote, on average, a greater proportion of their total capital expenditure to Taxonomy-aligned activities than to fossil fuel expansion.
Separately, the proposal preserves the alternative route under which Transition-category products may satisfy the 70% eligible investment threshold by investing at least 15% of their portfolio in EU Taxonomy-aligned activities. For sustainable-category products, however, the proposal increases the corresponding minimum allocation to EU Taxonomy-aligned activities from 15% to 20%.
The ECON committee has also proposed additional disclosure requirements for ESG Basics products. Under the proposal, such products would be required to identify and disclose the principal adverse impacts of their investments on sustainability factors, explain any measures taken to prevent, mitigate or remediate those impacts, and disclose the proportion of their investments in companies active in the fossil fuel sector.
In addition, the proposal narrows the Commission’s original exclusion criteria applicable to the Sustainable, Transition and ESG Basics categories. Whereas the Commission’s text excluded companies from eligibility wherever a benchmark administrator had found any violation of the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises or the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the ECON committee proposal would apply the exclusion only where the violation constitutes a severe breach of human rights or international humanitarian law that has not been effectively addressed and, where appropriate, remediated.
The ECON committee position also provides for an opt-out from the sustainability product categorisation regime for AIFs marketed exclusively to per se MiFID professional investors, provided that appropriate disclosures are included in the AIF’s pre-contractual documentation. The opt-out would not be available where an AIF is also marketed to elective professional investors or where any retail investor has access to the fund, and does not extend to UCITS funds or other financial products. This approach reflects a policy view that per se professional investors generally possess the expertise, experience and resources necessary to assess sustainability-related product characteristics without relying on the SFDR categorisation framework to the same extent as retail investors. By limiting the opt-out to AIFs marketed exclusively to per se professional investors, the proposal seeks to preserve the investor protection objectives where less sophisticated investor categories may be involved.
Although the Parliament broadly endorses the Commission’s proposed three-category framework, a number of differences between the Parliament’s position and the Council’s negotiating mandate of 24 June 2026 remain to be resolved in trilogue. Key areas of divergence include the minimum EU Taxonomy-alignment threshold for Sustainable products (Parliament: 20%; Council: 15% for both Sustainable and Transition products), the detailed conditions governing fossil fuel exposure within the Transition category, and the treatment of public-sector bonds.
That said, the Parliament’s position has converged with the Council’s on several important issues. Both institutions are now more closely aligned on the length of the implementation period, the availability of an opt-out for AIFs marketed exclusively to professional investors, the grandfathering of existing closed-ended funds, and the introduction of transitional ramp-up periods to allow funds time to meet the 70% eligible investment threshold. This increased alignment should help narrow the range of outstanding issues and facilitate progress in the trilogue negotiations.
Next steps
Following the Parliament’s formal endorsement of the ECON committee report as its negotiating mandate, trilogue discussions with the Council and the Commission can now begin. The first trilogue meeting is expected to take place on 22 October 2026.
Timing and transitional considerations
A further area of uncertainty concerns the transition from the existing SFDR framework to the proposed SFDR 2.0 regime, including how products currently classified and disclosed under Articles 8 and 9 SFDR will transition to the new product categories. At this stage, the legislative proposals do not provide detailed transitional arrangements, and a number of implementation questions remain to be addressed in the final stages of the legislative process.
The Commission originally proposed an 18-month implementation period following the entry into force of the revised regime. However, both the Parliament and the Council have expressed support for a longer period of up to two years, reflecting concerns around operational readiness and the need to sequence the Level 1 legislative framework with the development of related Level 2 regulatory measures.
On current proposals, and assuming political agreement is reached by the end of 2026, market participants should anticipate a transition period of approximately two years before the new requirements become applicable. The revised SFDR framework is therefore expected to apply from late 2028, giving firms additional time to review existing product classifications, assess compliance with the new categorisation regime, and implement any required changes to disclosures, product governance arrangements and marketing materials.

articles.full_text:
The United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP17) opens next week in Yerevan, Armenia, running from 19 to 30 October.
Representing the EU, the European Commission will join global partners to accelerate action under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework — focusing on stepping up implementation, mobilising finance, and placing Indigenous Peoples and local communities at the centre of nature protection.
Ahead of the official opening, Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera will represent the Commission at the 'Leaders for Nature' Summit on 16 October, hosted by the Armenian COP17 Presidency. World leaders are expected to adopt the Yerevan Declaration, "Taking Action for Nature," reaffirming high-level political commitment to global biodiversity targets.
During the conference's High-Level Segment (27–28 October), Commissioner Jessika Roswall will lead the EU negotiating team, participate in high-level sessions, and launch a new initiative: Friends of Credits for Nature and Biodiversity.
“Nature is at the heart of our economy and our resilience. The EU is implementing ambitious policies to protect and restore nature and is a major supporter of biodiversity protection worldwide. We need to collectively accelerate the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework to ensure a future that is sustainable and resilient for all.”
Jessika Roswall, Commissioner for Environment, Water Resilience and a Competitive Circular Economy
Global implementation review
The EU is committed to implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) adopted in 2022 and is making significant progress towards its global biodiversity targets, putting in place a strong framework to protect and restore nature.
This year’s Global Review marks the first test of the new planning, monitoring, reporting, and review procedures — a process that will repeat at CBD COP19 in 2030. Through this review, we reaffirm our collective commitment to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and signal an urgent need to accelerate action across all 23 global targets.
Reaching these targets is essential to halting biodiversity loss, from protecting and managing 30% of Earth’s land, inland waters, and coastal and marine areas by 2030 to restoring degraded ecosystems and integrating biodiversity into all sectors and policies.
The science is clear: healthy ecosystems are essential for our economies, sustainable jobs, poverty eradication, health, and climate change mitigation and resilience.
“Yerevan should be the COP of proof, not only of promises. Healthy ecosystems are indispensable for climate resilience, water security, food security and long-term prosperity. Protecting and restoring biodiversity is not a cost. It is an investment in our future, our economies and the next generations.
Now it’s time to turn the ambition of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity framework into delivery.”
Teresa Ribera, Executive Vice-President for Clean, Just and Competitive Transition
Mobilising biodiversity finance
The EU remains fully committed to mobilising funds from public and private sources for biodiversity by 2030. Furthermore, the EU is on track to deliver on President von der Leyen’s 2021 pledge to double international biodiversity funding from €3.5 billion to €7 billion — focusing especially on the most vulnerable developing nations.
Looking ahead to the 2028–2034 period, the Commission has proposed earmarking 35% of the total EU budget and 30% of international financing under the Global Europe instrument for climate and environmental action.
The Friends of Credits for Nature and Biodiversity, a newly launched initiative during a high-level side event on 27 October, will aim to foster party-led exchanges on innovative financing for biodiversity. Nature credits are emerging as a key mechanism to leverage private investment alongside public funding, directly supporting both EU and global biodiversity targets.
The EU will also co-host a dedicated session on 19 October titled “The DSI Multilateral Mechanism & the Cali Fund: What Is Needed to Enable Early Operationalization?”.
Established at CBD COP16 in 2024, the Cali Fund aims to ensure the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from digital sequence information (DSI) on genetic resources. Companies that make use of DSI — particularly within the pharmaceutical, agrifood, and biotechnology sectors — are called upon to contribute to the fund, with the proceeds to be used for global biodiversity conservation, particularly within Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
The EU is strongly committed to ensuring the full and effective participation of Indigenous Peoples and local communities in CBD processes. This is particularly important for the modalities of the new dedicated Subsidiary Body created two years ago at COP16, to be agreed at COP17.
Background
The 17th Conference of the Parties under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) as well as the 12th Conference of the Parties serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (CP COP-MOP12) and the 6th Conference of the Parties serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing (NP COP-MOP6) are scheduled for 19 to 30 October in Yerevan, Armenia. Collectively, they are also referred to as the UN Biodiversity Conference 2026.
The EU appreciates Armenia’s impressive efforts at making COP17 a success, including the Leaders’ Summit, the High-Level Segment and the four Presidency initiatives for accelerating implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF).

The 24-Hour Eco-Routine: How Green Founders Seamlessly Blend Sustainable Living from Home to Office
For the modern small business owner, sustainability isn’t a corporate risk checklist—it’s a lifestyle. You don’t leave your values on your kitchen counter when you head out the door in the morning. Yet, keeping a green lifestyle seamless when transitioning from your personal life to your professional domain can feel like running two separate marathons.
The good news? The most impactful sustainable practices don’t require an enterprise budget or a compliance officer. They just require alignment.
Here is what a perfectly integrated, 24-hour green routine looks like for founders who want to do good, feel good, and unlock the hidden efficiencies of a sustainable lifestyle.
7:00 AM – The Mindful Launch
The day doesn’t start at the office; it starts with your personal footprint. Green founders are increasingly looking at their morning routines as the foundation for their business day.
- The Power Breakfast: Sourcing morning coffee and breakfast ingredients from local B-Corps or regenerative agriculture brands.
- The Digital Cleanse: Clearing out your email inbox and closing expired browser tabs over breakfast. (Massive data centers run on electricity; deleting digital clutter is a micro-way to reduce your invisible carbon footprint).
9:00 AM – The Conscious Commute
How you get to work sets the tone for your team. The energy transition is happening on Main Street through intentional transit choices.
- Micro-Mobility: Utilizing e-bikes or public transit for commutes under five miles.
- The EV Buffer: If driving is required, EV-owning founders are utilizing the morning commute to map out local community charging networks, showing clients and employees that green infrastructure is practically viable.
11:00 AM – The Low-Impact Workplace
Once at the shop, studio, or office, small switches yield massive psychological and operational dividends.
- Ditching the Standby Drain: Setting office equipment, printers, and secondary monitors to automatic “smart-strip” shutoffs. If it’s not being used, it shouldn’t be drawing power.
- The Ambient Shift: Optimizing natural light and introducing air-purifying plants. It lowers the energy bill, boosts team mood, and visually signals your workplace values to visiting clients.
1:00 PM – The “Closed-Loop” Lunch
Lunch is the ultimate testing ground for a small business’s waste philosophy.
- The Single-Use Ban: Replacing plastic cutlery and paper plates in the breakroom with real, mismatched ceramic mugs and silverware sourced from local thrift stores. It adds character and eliminates daily waste.
- Smarter Catering: When ordering lunch for client meetings, choosing local vendors who use compostable packaging or offer zero-waste delivery options.
RELATED ARTICLE: climate technologies and sustainable living
3:00 PM – The Value-Aligned Choice
Afternoon operations are where your lifestyle meets your ledger.
- The Supplier Audit: Spending 15 minutes reviewing your primary vendors. Are you buying shipping boxes from a company that prioritizes recycled materials? Are your cleaning supplies eco-friendly?
- The Local Micro-Action: Aligning with UN Sustainable Development Goal 12 (Responsible Consumption). This means repairing a piece of office equipment instead of throwing it out, or donating excess inventory to a local community center.
6:00 PM – Winding Down & Powering Off
Closing up shop shouldn’t mean leaving the lights on.
- The Smart Thermostat Pivot: Programing the workspace climate control to automatically drop or raise temperatures by 4–5 degrees the moment the team leaves.
- The Visual Reset: Turning off all non-essential aesthetic lighting. A dark storefront at night isn’t bad for business—it tells the neighborhood that you respect energy conservation.
9:00 PM – The Evening Reflection
Living sustainably means resting sustainably.
- The Green Capital Thought: As you wind down, consider where your business capital sleeps. Many eco-conscious founders are shifting their business checking accounts to community banks or green lenders that promise not to fund fossil fuel projects. Knowing your operational money is doing good while you sleep is the ultimate founder peace of mind.
