L&G, NTR Secure $385 Million First Close for European Clean Power Fund
- $385 million secured: L&G and NTR’s Clean Power Transition IV Fund reaches its first close, backed by four returning institutional investors.
- Three European acquisitions: Initial investments span Finland, Sweden, and Ireland, covering approximately 1.5 GW of clean power generation and grid support infrastructure.
- $770 billion annual investment opportunity: Europe’s electrification ambitions require substantial private capital for renewable generation, energy storage, and supporting infrastructure.
Global asset manager L&G and energy transition specialist NTR have secured approximately $385 million in commitments for their Clean Power Transition IV Fund. The investment strategy targets renewable energy generation and electrification infrastructure across Europe.
The fund expands the partners’ investment mandate beyond renewable generation to include battery storage and infrastructure supporting the electrification of transport, heating, and industry.
Four institutional investors from the previous fund have returned as cornerstone backers, providing early capital for the expanded strategy.
Expanding Investment Beyond Renewable Energy Generation
The new fund builds on L&G and NTR’s previous joint strategy, which reached its final close in March 2025. That vehicle raised more than $747 million for European clean power infrastructure.
Clean Power Transition IV broadens the investment scope to capture opportunities across Europe’s evolving electricity system.
Alongside renewable generation, the fund will target energy storage and infrastructure that enables greater electricity consumption across industrial and commercial sectors.
The strategy reflects growing demand for grid flexibility as European countries expand renewable capacity and reduce fossil fuel dependence.
Heather Mulahasani, Managing Director of Real Assets, Asset Management at L&G, said: “Infrastructure continues to be a cornerstone of global private markets investing, with no shortage of demand for clean power infrastructure. The launch of our second joint Fund with NTR answers this demand by evolving our clean power strategy and expanding the Global Real Assets offerings within L&G’s private markets platform. By combining our heritage and long-term investment expertise with complementary strengths from our strategic partners, we continue to deliver against our Asset Management growth ambitions while aiming to meet investor appetite for innovative, marketleading strategies with tangible real-world impacts.”
Three Acquisitions Establish European Investment Portfolio
The fund has completed three acquisitions across Finland, Sweden, and Ireland, establishing an initial portfolio spanning generation and storage infrastructure.
In Finland, the fund acquired Kandalos, a ready-to-build 125 MW battery energy storage project near Tornio. The facility will provide 250 MWh of storage capacity, with construction scheduled for 2026 and operations expected in 2027.
In Sweden, the acquisition of Vindr AB provides access to a development platform containing more than 1 GW of clean power projects. These projects span three electricity price regions and multiple development stages.
The third acquisition, Swordlestown in County Kildare, Ireland, combines 138 MWp of solar generation with a 200 MW battery storage system. The storage component will provide 400 MWh of capacity.
Together, the acquisitions establish approximately 1.5 GW of generation and grid support infrastructure.
Battery storage features across all three investments, reflecting its growing importance in balancing intermittent renewable generation and electricity demand.
RELATED ARTICLE: L&G Capital Appoints Julia Goldsworthy as Head of Social Impact Investment
Europe’s Electrification Targets Create Investment Demand
Europe’s energy transition requires substantial infrastructure investment beyond renewable generation.
L&G and NTR estimate that approximately $770 billion annually will be needed for clean power generation, electricity grids, electrification, and energy efficiency.
The estimate relates to the EU’s proposed ambition to electrify 46% of energy consumption by 2040.
Meeting that objective would require significant investment in electricity networks, storage capacity, and infrastructure connecting new demand to renewable supply.
Rosheen McGuckian, CEO of NTR, said: “Electrification is an integral part of the solution to drive the clean energy transition across our European markets. Decarbonising transport, heat and industry will require continued investment in clean power generation alongside the storage, grid and connection infrastructure that enables it, creating a substantial opportunity for institutional capital.”
Institutional Capital Targets Europe’s Energy Security
L&G and NTR have collaborated since 2015, when L&G became a cornerstone investor in NTR’s first two funds.
Their latest strategy combines NTR’s project origination and asset management expertise with L&G’s institutional investment capabilities.
For investors, the expanded mandate offers exposure to multiple infrastructure segments supporting European decarbonisation.
The strategy also introduces varying development, construction, and operational risks across its portfolio.
Europe’s ability to attract long-term private capital will remain central to delivering the infrastructure required for energy security and industrial electrification.
The fund’s first close demonstrates continued institutional interest in financing that transition, particularly where renewable generation and grid flexibility investments can support long-term returns.

ESG News Week In Review: 01 September – 15 September
AI power demand stopped being a forecast and started writing cheques. Google committed $15.1 billion to Finland behind a 22-year nuclear contract, strategic buyers paid $8.5 billion for cooling and power conversion, and regulators in Brussels and London moved the other way on disclosure.
The fortnight’s defining trade was electricity for compute. Google committed at least $15.1 billion to Finnish AI infrastructure behind a 22-year power purchase agreement for up to half the output of Fortum’s Loviisa nuclear plant, its largest European investment. Days later the US Department of Energy closed a $1.9 billion loan to restart the 615 MW Duane Arnold reactor in Iowa, with Google as the plant’s primary customer and 2029 the target. Firm nuclear output is becoming the balance sheet item that makes a data centre financeable.
The acquisition market made the same argument from the supply side. SLB agreed to pay about $4.1 billion for Kelvion’s thermal management business, Flex agreed $4.4 billion for EPC Power, and Blackstone moved on liquid cooling supplier Flow Control Holdings. The binding constraint on AI buildout is no longer chips but heat rejection and grid-compatible power, and strategic buyers are now paying control premiums to own it.
Regulators moved in the opposite direction. The European Parliament’s ECON Committee backed an SFDR position that would let fossil fuel companies expanding production qualify for the proposed transition category, and would exempt some professional-investor products from disclosure altogether. The UK opened a consultation that would remove explicit strategic-report duties covering environmental impact, workforce, diversity and human rights. A federal judge blocked New York’s $75 billion Climate Change Superfund Act as preempted by federal law, stalling the theory that states can bill historic emitters and putting Vermont’s contested statute in doubt.
The story to carry into next week is the EPA repeal. Bloomberg reported on 14 September that federal carbon standards for coal and gas power plants could be struck within days, rules projected to prevent a billion tonnes of emissions by 2047. The electricity sector is close to a quarter of US greenhouse gas pollution, so if the standards fall, every utility climate plan and every investor model priced against them has to be rewritten.

articles.full_text:
France, Germany Near Deal to Ease EU 2035 Car Emissions Targets
- EU emissions targets: France and Germany are nearing an agreement to reduce the EU’s 2035 car emissions target to 90%, removing additional compensation requirements.
- UK market access: Britain could qualify for preferential treatment under EU “Made in Europe” rules, subject to reciprocal trade and investment conditions.
- Automotive competitiveness: The proposed changes could ease compliance costs for European automakers while reshaping clean vehicle investment and supply chain policies.
France and Germany Move Toward Automotive Policy Compromise
France and Germany are nearing an agreement to ease the European Union’s 2035 vehicle emissions requirements while expanding preferential market access for Britain.
The proposed compromise would reduce regulatory pressure on European automakers and reshape the bloc’s industrial competitiveness strategy. However, the agreement remains provisional and requires broader EU approval.
Diplomats said the two countries are close to resolving disagreements over vehicle emissions targets and European manufacturing requirements.
The negotiations come as European automakers face mounting pressure from electrification costs, international competition and tightening environmental regulations.
At stake is the balance between protecting Europe’s automotive industry and maintaining its long-term climate commitments.
EU Car Emissions Target Could Fall to 90%
The European Commission previously proposed a 90% reduction in car CO2 emissions by 2035, measured against 2021 levels.
Under that proposal, manufacturers would need to compensate for the remaining 10% through low-carbon steel and alternative fuels. These measures would effectively bridge the gap toward a 100% reduction.
The emerging Franco-German agreement would retain the 90% emissions reduction target but eliminate the additional compensation requirements.
This approach broadly aligns with the preferences of German automakers, which have sought greater flexibility in meeting future emissions standards.
For manufacturers, removing compensation obligations could reduce compliance costs and provide more flexibility in vehicle technology and production strategies.
However, the proposal would also weaken the original framework’s overall emissions ambition.
Germany faces additional domestic political complications. The country’s Social Democratic environment minister has suggested an alternative requiring a 95% emissions reduction.
Under that approach, low-carbon steel would compensate for the remaining five percentage points.
These competing positions illustrate the political difficulty of reconciling industrial competitiveness with Europe’s climate objectives.
Britain Could Gain Access to EU Manufacturing Incentives
The negotiations also address proposed EU rules governing local-content and low-carbon requirements in public procurement, auctions and subsidy programmes.
France has advocated restricting eligible products to those manufactured within the EU’s 27 member states.
Germany and several other countries favour a broader definition that includes closely integrated trading partners.
The provisional agreement would extend automotive eligibility under “Made in Europe” provisions to European partners participating in the EU internal market on January 1, 2020.
This definition would include Britain, which formally left the EU single market at the end of 2020.
For British automotive manufacturers, inclusion could preserve access to European industrial incentives and procurement opportunities.
It could also support established cross-border supply chains serving vehicle manufacturers across Britain and continental Europe.
However, preferential treatment would not be unconditional.

Trade Reciprocity and Chinese EV Restrictions Remain Critical
The proposed agreement requires “full reciprocity” alongside “dynamic alignment with EU conditions for investment from third countries and with EU trade protection measures”.
These provisions could require Britain to align with European restrictions targeting Chinese-manufactured hybrid and battery electric vehicles.
Such conditions would connect industrial subsidy eligibility with broader EU trade defence policies.
For automotive executives and investors, the implications extend beyond manufacturing location.
Companies could face additional considerations involving supply chain exposure, investment screening and compliance with European trade measures.
The proposed framework could also influence future decisions about battery manufacturing, vehicle assembly and sourcing strategies.
EU Approval Remains the Final Hurdle
A Franco-German agreement would provide political momentum but would not automatically change EU legislation.
Both countries must secure support from other member states and the European Parliament before the proposals can enter into force.
Negotiations could prove difficult as governments weigh domestic manufacturing interests against emissions reduction commitments.
For investors, the outcome will influence long-term assumptions about electric vehicle demand, automotive capital expenditure and low-carbon materials.
The wider implications extend to Europe’s industrial policy credibility. Policymakers must balance regulatory flexibility with the investment certainty needed to support decarbonisation.
The final agreement could determine how Europe protects its automotive competitiveness while pursuing climate objectives and managing increasingly complex international trade relationships.

articles.full_text:
American Electric Power to Invest $4 Billion in Google Fuel Cell Project
- $4 billion investment: American Electric Power (AEP) plans a 702-megawatt fuel cell facility in Wyoming to supply Google’s expanding data center operations.
- 20-year power agreement: The project will use Bloom Energy technology, with construction expected to begin in 2026 and full operations targeted for late 2028.
- Growing AI energy demand: The investment follows Google’s separate agreement with Black Hills Corp, highlighting the increasing need for dedicated electricity infrastructure.
American Electric Power (AEP) plans to invest approximately $4 billion in a major fuel cell project near Cheyenne, Wyoming, to supply electricity to Google’s expanding data center operations.
The 702-megawatt facility will operate under a 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Alphabet’s Google. The investment comes as technology companies seek reliable electricity supplies to support artificial intelligence and cloud computing infrastructure.
AEP shares rose more than 3.1% in premarket trading following the announcement, reflecting investor interest in utilities benefiting from accelerating data center demand.
The project will use fuel cell technology developed by Bloom Energy, providing on-demand electricity while reducing reliance on conventional grid expansion.
AEP Expands Energy Infrastructure for Google’s Data Centers
Cheyenne Fuel Cell will develop the facility, with AEP holding approximately 92% ownership. Funds advised by Basalt Infrastructure Partners will retain the remaining stake.
Construction is scheduled to begin in 2026, with full commercial operations expected by the end of 2028.
The facility will supply Google’s growing electricity requirements in the Cheyenne area. Its 702 MW capacity provides a substantial source of dedicated generation for energy-intensive computing operations.
The 20-year PPA also establishes a long-term commercial relationship between the utility and Google. Such agreements can provide revenue visibility for infrastructure investors while helping technology companies secure future electricity supplies.
For AEP, the investment expands its exposure to the rapidly growing data center electricity market.
However, the project’s financial performance will depend on construction costs, technology reliability and the terms governing electricity delivery.
Google Secures Additional Power Through Black Hills Agreement
The AEP investment follows another major electricity agreement involving Google’s proposed Cheyenne data center.
Earlier this month, Google signed a similar arrangement with Black Hills Corp to support its regional operations.
Under that agreement, Black Hills plans to invest approximately $1.8 billion in new electricity generation capacity between 2027 and 2029.
Together, the two arrangements demonstrate the scale of infrastructure investment associated with expanding AI computing capacity.
Technology companies increasingly face constraints from limited grid capacity, lengthy infrastructure development schedules and rising electricity demand.
Dedicated generation projects offer an alternative route to securing power, particularly where traditional grid upgrades cannot match the pace of data center construction.
However, these arrangements also raise questions about energy costs, grid integration and the environmental performance of new electricity supplies.
RELATED ARTICLE: Google Backs Texas Electric Freight Route
Bloom Energy Technology Supports On-Demand Generation
AEP’s planned facility will use fuel cells developed by Bloom Energy, extending an existing commercial relationship between the companies.
In January, AEP exercised an option to purchase a substantial portion of up to 900 MW of additional Bloom fuel cells. The agreement was valued at approximately $2.65 billion.
Fuel cell systems generate electricity through electrochemical processes rather than conventional combustion. They can provide continuous power without depending on intermittent renewable electricity generation.
Their environmental performance, however, depends heavily on the fuel source and associated upstream emissions.
The announcement did not specify the proposed Wyoming facility’s fuel supply, emissions profile or renewable energy integration arrangements.
These details will be important when assessing the project’s contribution to Google’s broader climate commitments.
For corporate sustainability teams, reliable electricity procurement must increasingly balance operational resilience, affordability and emissions reduction.
AI Electricity Demand Reshapes Utility Investment Strategies
The proposed investment reflects a broader shift in electricity infrastructure planning as utilities respond to large technology customers.
Long-term PPAs can help support capital-intensive generation projects by establishing predictable demand over extended periods.
For investors, the AEP arrangement creates exposure to AI-driven electricity growth while introducing construction, operational and technology risks.
The project’s ownership structure also illustrates how infrastructure investment partnerships can support large-scale generation development.
From an ESG perspective, the central issue extends beyond securing sufficient electricity.
Technology companies must also evaluate the carbon intensity of new generation, potential grid impacts and consistency with corporate decarbonization commitments.
For utilities, meeting demand from hyperscale data centers will require substantial capital allocation and careful management of regulatory and environmental obligations.
AEP’s $4 billion project adds to a growing pipeline of dedicated electricity investments supporting AI infrastructure. Its development will provide an important test of how utilities and technology companies balance energy security, commercial returns and climate objectives as global computing demand accelerates.

articles.full_text:
Mars Impact Fund Commits $3 Million to Expand Youth Science Careers Across US
- $3 million investment: Mars Impact Fund will support National 4-H Council’s Beyond Ready initiative over three years, expanding access to science education and career development.
- 200,000 young people targeted: The partnership will create career pathways in food science, agriculture and veterinary medicine through six university-led programs.
- Long-term workforce development: The investment supports Beyond Ready’s ambition to equip 10 million young people with career-ready skills by 2030.
Mars Incorporated has committed $3 million over three years to expand science education and career opportunities for young people across the United States.
Announced in McLean, Virginia, the partnership between Mars Impact Fund and National 4-H Council will support up to 200,000 young people. It focuses on developing future talent in food science, agriculture and veterinary medicine, sectors facing growing demand for specialized skills.
The funding will strengthen National 4-H Council’s Beyond Ready initiative, which aims to prepare 10 million young people for employment and life by 2030.
For Mars, the investment connects corporate philanthropy with long-term workforce development across industries central to its global operations.
Addressing Workforce Needs in Food and Agriculture
The initiative targets career pathways that support food production, agricultural innovation and animal health.
As food systems face mounting pressure from climate change, resource constraints and evolving consumer demand, access to skilled professionals remains critical.
Mars intends to address these challenges by introducing young people to scientific careers through practical education, mentorship and industry exposure.
“As a family-owned business for 115 years, Mars thinks in generations, prioritizing innovation and inspiring youth to pursue careers in science,” said Michelle Grogg, Executive Director of the Mars Impact Fund.
“Demand for skilled talent in food science, agriculture and veterinary medicine continues to grow and we want to be sure that young people have the opportunity to explore those careers. We are proud to partner with the National 4-H Council to advance that goal, and help equip the next generation with education, experiences and mentorship.”
The investment also reflects the growing importance of workforce readiness within corporate social impact strategies.
Six Universities to Deliver Regional Science Programs
Funding will flow through 4-H’s Cooperative Extension network, which connects communities with educational resources from more than 100 public universities.
Six university partnerships will deliver programs tailored to regional workforce needs.
The University of California will establish a mobile veterinary education laboratory serving teenagers in Monterey and Santa Barbara Counties.
Florida A&M University will introduce agricultural science workshops and academies covering livestock production, entomology and emerging agricultural technologies.
The University of Georgia will develop a statewide career-readiness pathway connecting agricultural education with professional experience.
Meanwhile, the University of Illinois will focus on practical workforce skills across food, agricultural and veterinary sciences.
Michigan State University will emphasize animal health, food security and agricultural systems.
The University of Tennessee will establish a year-round veterinary science program incorporating virtual learning, field visits and industry partnerships.
Together, the programs aim to make scientific careers more accessible while strengthening connections between education and employment.
RELATED ARTICLE: Mars Reaches 98% Responsible Cocoa Sourcing
Scholarships Expand Access to Career Development
Beyond university programming, the partnership will fund 20 full scholarships annually for teenagers attending National 4-H Council’s Ignite summit.
The event provides opportunities to explore careers, develop leadership capabilities and build professional networks.
“Young people are curious about science, and seeing themselves in these careers starts with having the opportunity to experience them firsthand,” said Heather Elliott, Chief Development & Marketing Officer, National 4-H Council.
“Through the Beyond Ready initiative, we’re helping 10 million young people develop the problem-solving, communication and technical skills they need to succeed in work and life, including pursuing careers in food, agriculture and veterinary science. Working with Mars allows us to connect those career-ready skills to real pathways and help more young people see where their interests can take them.”
Corporate Philanthropy Linked to Long-Term Resilience
The commitment expands Mars Impact Fund’s global philanthropic portfolio, which has exceeded $20 million in commitments since launching earlier in 2026.
For corporate leaders and ESG investors, the partnership illustrates how social investment can support workforce development alongside business resilience.
Building scientific expertise across agriculture, food systems and veterinary medicine can strengthen the talent pipeline for industries navigating environmental and technological change.
The initiative also places measurable outcomes at the center of corporate philanthropy, with defined funding, participation targets and delivery partners.
Its longer-term value will depend on whether educational access translates into sustained career opportunities.
For global food and agriculture businesses, developing future scientific talent remains an important component of resilient supply chains and sustainable economic growth.
